source.title: Triple descent and the two kinds of overfitting: where and why do they appear?
source.authors: Stéphane d'Ascoli; Levent Sagun; G. Biroli

record.file_problem: The text includes some PDF-extraction artifacts in equations and figure layouts, but the paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests sample-wise, parameter-wise, and training-time test-loss behavior in random-feature and teacher-student neural-network settings, using a different setup from the original studies; it also refines the account by distinguishing two peaks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-loss sweeps and training-time results. Results cited from other work are not included as rows. Hyperparameter and activation choices used to define experiments are recorded as conditions, not as standalone outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own test-loss sweeps over sample count N and parameter count P. These cover random-feature regression (analytical and numerical) and 3-layer teacher-student networks trained by gradient descent. It finds sample-wise and parameter-wise peaks at interpolation, then splits the sample-wise peak into a linear peak (N=D) and a nonlinear peak (N=P), with noise, nonlinearity, regularization and ensembling dependence. Neither original source is this paper.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Additions: the nonlinear peak at N=P survives without noise and can be suppressed by regularization or ensembling. The linear peak at N=D comes solely from fitting label noise, is implicitly regularized by the nonlinearity, and forms earlier during training.
record.recipe_differences: Uses test-loss sweeps over parameter count and sample count, plus teacher-student neural networks and random-feature theory. The regression task, phase-space analysis, and training setup differ from the original studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with signal-to-noise ratio, activation nonlinearity, explicit regularization, ensembling, training time, and data structure.

fits_no_version.finding: The linear peak forms early in gradient-descent training, while the nonlinear peak forms only late, as the slow small-eigenvalue modes are learned.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different double-descent peaks emerge on different training timescales.

record.problems: The numerical neural-network experiments use a teacher-student regression setup; results are averaged over 10 runs but uncertainty estimates are not reported. Many plotted values are not tabulated. Training-time results use selected phase-space snapshots rather than complete fixed-model epoch trajectories.

untested.parts: There is no explicit model-size sweep for the deep (3-layer) networks; only the joint (P,N) phase space at SNR=0.2 is shown. No standard deep architectures are tested.
No test-error-versus-epoch curve for a fixed model is reported.
Only random-feature regression is tested as a non-deep model class. Kernels, trees and other classes are not tested.
The paper does not test whether a single complexity measure predicts peak locations. It only invokes effective model complexity to explain the CIFAR10 peak shift.
Optimally tuned regularization is not tested; only fixed regularization strengths are used.
Complexity is not re-counted with an effective-parameter measure.

missing.what: NN phase space at SNR=0.2 shows an N=P overfitting line, i.e. a parameter-wise peak in a 3-layer network.
RF on downsampled MNIST still shows the linear peak at N=D and the nonlinear peak at N=P.
Sample-wise RF profiles across r and SNR: the linear peak appears only at high noise with r>0.8; the nonlinear peak is always visible for r<1.

record.verdict_notes: On CIFAR10 the authors explain the nonlinear peak's shift with training time by effective model complexity, a cited idea, not a test of V5. The reader validation issue (r4 linked to V4) is resolved by restricting the V4 label to r1. The study is mostly theoretical; the NN experiments are small (D=196) and report no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: Tests parameter-wise behavior in the reported random-feature setting; the neural-network experiments primarily report joint parameter/sample phase spaces rather than a separate size sweep.
Reports test-loss phase spaces at selected training times, not a single fixed model's complete test-error curve over every epoch.
Tests sample-size effects in noisy regression settings, including random-feature, neural-network, and structured-data experiments; not all datasets or noise regimes are covered.
Tests random-feature and neural-network examples, not a broad range of model classes.
The paper invokes effective model complexity when discussing cited work, but does not test whether one measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Studies noise, activation nonlinearity, multiple peaks, ensembling, and regularization; it does not establish behavior under optimally tuned regularization.
Does not re-count complexity using an effective parameter measure or test whether that turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: RF model
rows.operation_detail: Swept parameter count and measured test loss as a function of P.
rows.value: The parameter-wise profile exhibits double descent, with an overfitting line at N = P.
rows.note: The paper describes the parameter-wise double-descent profile; the plotted loss values are not tabulated.
rows.check: The RF model is a two-layer network with a fixed random first layer, not a deep network. It bears on V4 (another model class), not V1.

rows.subject: RF model
rows.operation_detail: Swept parameter count in the parameter-wise test-loss profile.
rows.measure: Test loss as parameter count varies
rows.value: The parameter-wise profile is monotonically decreasing in the linear case r = 1.
rows.locator: Appendix A, Fig. 10 and accompanying text
rows.note: The reported monotone decrease does not show parameter-wise double descent for this linear case.
rows.check: With r=1 the features have rank at most D, below N (N/D=10). The model never reaches interpolation as P grows, so a monotone curve cannot show whether risk improves past interpolation. Not a failure of double descent; drop V1.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix A.1, Fig. 10; Sec. 2.2, linear-component rank.

rows.subject: RF model
rows.size_stated: P/D = 10 in the spectral example; other phase-space sizes not stated
rows.operation_detail: Swept training sample count and measured test loss.
rows.value: The sample-wise profile has peaks at N = D and N = P (triple descent).
rows.note: The paper states that the N = D peak is most salient at high noise and that both peaks can occur together.
rows.check: This is a sample-wise sweep, not a capacity sweep, so V4 does not apply.

rows.subject: NN model
rows.size_stated: 3-layer fully connected student; 100 nodes per layer not stated for the student
rows.stage_stated: trained with gradient descent for 1000 epochs; selected checkpoints also shown
rows.operation_detail: Swept training sample count and measured test loss in a teacher-student regression task.
rows.value: The phase space shows a qualitatively similar triple-descent situation, with lines N = D and N = P.
rows.note: Results are averaged over 10 initialization runs.

rows.subject: NN model
rows.stage_stated: training checkpoints at t = 26, 78, 233, and 695 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Measured test-loss phase spaces at selected points during gradient-descent training.
rows.measure: Test-loss phase space and emergence of the N = D and N = P peaks
rows.value: The linear peak appears early and persists; the nonlinear peak forms later in training.
rows.note: The paper reports development of peaks across phase spaces at selected epochs, not a complete fixed-model test-error trajectory.
rows.check: These are phase-space snapshots at four epochs showing when each sample-wise peak forms. No fixed model's test error over epochs is reported, so a fall-rise-fall in time cannot be read.

rows.subject: NN model
rows.stage_stated: training checkpoints at t = 23, 138, 832, and 4999 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Measured test-loss phase spaces during training on structured data.
rows.measure: Test loss across sample counts and selected training times
rows.value: At late times, a broad overfitting region appears at N < D; the nonlinear peak shifts to higher N during training and scales sublinearly with P.
rows.locator: Appendix C, Fig. 15a and accompanying text
rows.note: This structured-data result differs from a fixed peak at N = P and shows multiple linear peaks in the discussion.
rows.check: Sample-wise overfitting persists on CIFAR10, but its location differs (broad region at N<D; nonlinear peak at N~P^α, α<1). The peak shift over training is not an epoch-wise test-error curve, so drop V2. The state is observed rather than partial.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix C.2, Fig. 15a and discussion of linear and nonlinear peaks.

rows.subject: RF model
rows.operation_detail: Compared sample-wise test loss in noisy and noiseless settings.
rows.measure: Test loss and its bias-variance components as N varies
rows.value: The linear peak at N = D vanishes in the noiseless setup; the nonlinear peak remains, with initialization variance contributing to it.
rows.note: The paper attributes the linear peak solely to label-noise variance and the nonlinear peak to initialization and noise variance.

rows.subject: RF model
rows.operation_detail: Compared test-loss profiles with and without averaging over independently initialized models.
rows.value: Ensembling mitigates the nonlinear peak but does not affect the linear peak.
rows.note: The authors describe the effect as mitigation, not elimination.
rows.check: The row measures how ensembling changes the peaks, which bears on V6. Drop V3.

rows.subject: RF model
rows.operation_detail: Compared test-loss profiles under increased ridge regularization.
rows.value: Increasing regularization mitigates the nonlinear peak but does not affect the linear peak.
rows.note: The study does not report an optimally tuned regularization sweep.
rows.check: Only two ridge values are compared (1e-5 vs 1e-3), with no optimal tuning. Drop V3.

rows.subject: NN model
rows.operation_detail: Compared test-loss phase spaces with ensembling and weight decay.
rows.value: Ensembling and regularizing attenuate the nonlinear peak more than the linear peak.
rows.note: The plotted panels compare vanilla, ensemble, and weight-decay settings; the text characterizes the nonlinear peak as more affected.
rows.check: The row measures attenuation of the peaks by ensembling and weight decay. Drop V3.

rows.subject: RF model
rows.operation_detail: Compared sample-wise test-loss profiles across activation nonlinearities.
rows.measure: Test loss as N varies; relative peak strength
rows.value: Increasing nonlinearity strengthens the nonlinear peak and weakens the linear peak; the linear peak is most evident for weakly nonlinear activations at high noise.
rows.note: The text reports the direction of the change, while the plotted peak values are not tabulated.

source_check.locator_found: Sec. 3.1, Fig. 7 and caption; Appendix A.1, Figs. 10–11.

rows.subject: NN model
rows.operation_detail: Compared sample-wise loss profiles with Tanh and ReLU activations.
rows.measure: Test-loss phase space and relative linear-peak strength
rows.value: Both peaks remain visible with ReLU, but the linear peak is much weaker than with Tanh.
rows.note: This is reported as consistent with stronger nonlinearity weakening the linear peak.
rows.check: Both peaks remain and the linear peak weakens with stronger nonlinearity, as the dependence predicts. The state should be observed, not partial. Fig. 12 uses weight decay γ=0.05, which the row omits from its conditions.

source_check.correct: Both activation conditions in Fig. 12 use weight decay γ=0.05.
source_check.problem: The condition omits the weight decay used for this activation comparison.
